A1.justification: Both PDFs describe L2G-Net by the same authors. The complete main texts, figures, tables, algorithms, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic runtime experiments, L2G-Net results on four heterophilous datasets, and a Minesweeper attribution analysis.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds molecular and City-Networks evaluations, timing and memory results, and spectral and attribution diagnostics.

M1.justification: The factorization algorithms and core hierarchical spectral layer remain unchanged. v2 adds an inductive adaptation sharing filter banks across subgraphs at the same level and evaluates positional-encoding variants. It also specifies B-spline filters for every dataset, whereas v1 explicitly used RBF filters for Tolokers.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained synthetic experiments and four heterophilous datasets, v2 evaluates peptides-func and peptides-struct as inductive molecular graph prediction tasks and Paris, Shanghai, Los Angeles, and London as much larger transductive graphs. These substantially expand task, domain, and scale coverage.

E2.justification: The original heterophily accuracy comparison retains its comparator set. New comparisons introduce methods including Specformer, Graph ViT, GRIT, and S2GCN on peptides, and SGFormer, GCNII, and DropEdge on City-Networks (Tables 13–14). Tables 10–11 also add training-time comparisons against GCN, ChebNet, and Polynormer.

E3.justification: v2 adds unsparsified peptide evaluation using AP and MAE, deeper City-Networks hierarchies with stated cut sparsification, 64-bit memory comparisons, and training-time comparisons with matched depth and hidden dimensions for selected baselines. The reported Tolokers filter basis changes from RBF to B-spline; this does not establish that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds impulse-response locality analysis (Figure 2), eigengap diagnostics concerning deflation (Figure 7), learned-filter analysis (Figure 9), and peptide comparisons with and without positional encodings. It extends the existing Minesweeper Grad-CAM analysis to the other three heterophilous datasets (Figure 10). These investigate mechanisms and behavior beyond additional benchmark scores.

E5.justification: City-Networks results explicitly report means and standard deviations over four random seeds. The original ten-partition heterophily reporting, three-run synthetic timing summaries, and attribution confidence-interval practice are retained. There is no reported increase in replication for the original experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds peptide and city scores, memory requirements, training times, and diagnostic findings. Examples include peptide AP 72.14 and MAE 0.2479, and London factorization time 144.22 minutes; the corresponding ED runtime is projected because ED runs out of memory. The retained Amazon-ratings result changes from 53.41±1.34 to 53.39±0.58; other original accuracy and decomposition-time entries remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1 and Appendix G add a strict-containment argument comparing L2G-Net with global spectral filters, including a two-node counterexample. Theorem 4.1 changes the cut-size bound from O(n log n/epsilon^2) to O(epsilon^-2) and the construction cost from O(n log n) to O(|E| log n). Appendix F also revises the merging-complexity derivation and discusses quadratic-cost matrix products.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—exact factorization, advantageous graph partitioning, and L2G-Net—remain intact. v2's abstract explicitly claims scalability beyond standard GFT feasibility, and its introduction extends the claimed empirical applicability to inductive tasks and larger transductive graphs. These refine the contribution's reach without replacing its central premise.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of task-dependent learned filters, positional encodings as complementary, and the tradeoff between per-epoch cost and convergence time. It explicitly recommends polynomial filters or message passing when linear complexity is essential, discusses dynamic and signed graphs, and leaves directed graphs for future work. These materially expand mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix C and Table 8 provide hyperparameters for six added datasets, including hierarchy depths, learning rates, dropout, and training steps. v2 also discloses a 10^-12 deflation threshold and memory precision. Conversely, it omits v1's filter-bank counts and learnable-center formulation; those omissions do not establish that the corresponding mechanisms were removed.

R1.justification: The expanded related work in Appendix B adds substantive positioning against hybrid spatial-spectral GNNs and classical and HSS divide-and-conquer eigensolvers, including Cuppen, Gu and Eisenstat, and Ou and Xia. It reframes positional encodings as complementary and removes v1's assertion that optimizing earlier GFT factorizations is NP-hard. These exceed citation metadata updates.

P1.justification: v2 extensively revises the introduction and explanatory narrative, moves related work from Section 2.3 to Appendix B, and reorganizes experiments around separate transductive, inductive, locality, and memory discussions. It adds dedicated expressiveness and intuition appendices and broadly replaces 'interface' terminology with 'cut'.

P2.justification: v2 adds a positioning table, multiple benchmark and efficiency tables, and figures for impulse propagation, eigengaps, a barbell graph, learned filters, and additional attribution curves. The hyperparameter table gains hierarchy levels and loses bank-count and basis columns. Original runtime, parameter-performance, and Minesweeper attribution graphics are retained and renumbered; Figure 1 receives a visual refinement.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by testing unsparsified inductive molecular tasks and much larger, sparsified city graphs, directly examining previously untested applicability and scalability. Added efficiency and locality analyses make practical benefits and costs substantially more assessable. The stronger Theorem 4.1 bound lacks a corresponding new supporting derivation, and some filter specifications are lost, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in direct validation, research positioning, and explicit applicability limits.
